title: From Amritsar's Bylanes to Harvard's Stage: Vikas Khanna Named Person of the Year
excerpt: Harvard's South Asian Association honors the Michelin-starred chef, filmmaker, and TIME 100 inductee — a crowning moment in a year that has redefined what Indian cuisine means on the world stage.
body:
Vikas Khanna stood at the podium at Harvard University and did what he does best: he made an entrance that nobody could ignore. The South Asian Association (SAA) of Harvard had just named him Person of the Year — and the chef, who grew up in the tight bylanes of Amritsar, was struggling to hold back tears.

"No words to express my feelings today — from the bylanes of Amritsar to the stage at Harvard University," Khanna said. "Thank you, Boston, for so much love. Heading back to New York with a full heart."

## A Year Like No Other

The Harvard honor is the latest in a cascade of recognition that has turned 2026 into Vikas Khanna's annus mirabilis. In April, TIME magazine named him to its 2026 list of the 100 Most Influential People in the World — a citation written by none other than James Beard Award-winning chef and Le Bernardin co-owner Eric Ripert. In May, Mumbai's RPH College of Hospitality Management launched the Chef Vikas Khanna Scholarship in his name, a new academic excellence initiative for aspiring hospitality students.

The Harvard SAA's honor celebrates what Khanna has spent three decades building: a global platform for Indian cuisine that transcends the kitchen. He is not merely a chef. He is a cultural ambassador who has used food, film, and philanthropy to reshape how the world sees India's culinary heritage.

## The Journey

Khanna's story is one the diaspora knows well — it is, in many ways, their story too. Born in Amritsar, raised in a Punjabi household where the kitchen was the spiritual center of family life, he grew up watching his grandmother cook with an intuition that no culinary school could teach. He arrived in New York with little more than a suitcase and a conviction that Indian food deserved a seat at the world's finest tables.

The road was brutal. Khanna slept on floors, worked in tiny kitchens, and endured the kind of rejection that would have sent most people home. But he stayed. And he cooked. And eventually, New York noticed. His restaurant Junoon held a Michelin star for eight consecutive years. His latest venture, Bungalow in Manhattan — a Michelin Bib Gourmand recipient — has become a cultural tribute to India, celebrating its heritage through an immersive dining experience that treats every meal as storytelling.

## Beyond the Kitchen

What sets Khanna apart from his peers is the breadth of his ambition. He has authored more than 41 books documenting India's culinary traditions. His directorial debut, *The Last Color*, earned international acclaim. His humanitarian initiative, Feed India, distributed more than 30 million meals across 135 cities during the COVID-19 pandemic through his South Asian Kid's Infinite Vision foundation.

As a judge on Celebrity MasterChef India, he has inspired a generation of young chefs across the country, bringing the same intensity and warmth to television that he brings to his restaurants.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs, Khanna's Harvard recognition carries a particular weight. It is one thing for a chef to win accolades in the food world. It is another for an academic institution of Harvard's stature to recognize what Indian cuisine represents — not just as food, but as culture, identity, and a bridge between civilizations.

"This recognition is not just an award — it's a promise," Khanna said. "A commitment to continue honoring our culture through every dish, every detail."

In a year when Indian chefs are earning Michelin stars, James Beard nominations, and a place on every food trend list in America, Khanna's Harvard honor feels less like a surprise and more like a coronation. Indian cuisine has always been worthy. In 2026, the rest of the world is finally keeping up.

## What's Next

Khanna shows no signs of slowing down. His new film *Imaginary Rain*, a culinary-focused drama set in New York, is slated for release later this year. And at Bungalow, the reservations remain as hard to get as ever — a small, satisfying measure of how far a boy from Amritsar's bylanes can travel when he refuses to stop cooking.
